title: Iran Just Threatened to Close a Second Chokepoint. For India, the Red Sea Route Was Supposed to Be the Backup Plan.
excerpt: The IRGC says it will shut 'all other export corridors' as Houthi allies warn of $200 oil. India's alternative shipping routes through the Suez Canal are now at risk.
body:
The Strait of Hormuz was the crisis. The Red Sea was the workaround. Now Iran is threatening to take both off the table.

In a statement carried by state news agency IRNA on Wednesday, Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps declared it would close "all other export corridors that benefit the U.S. and its allies" — a thinly veiled threat to deploy its Houthi proxies to shut the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, the narrow gateway linking the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden.

"Regional energy exports are either shared by all, or denied to all," the IRGC said.

The threat comes as the U.S. reimposed a full naval blockade of Iranian ports and launched a fresh wave of strikes — seven hours of precision attacks targeting Iranian coastal defenses, missile sites, and maritime capabilities near the Strait of Hormuz. Iran has attacked seven commercial ships in the past week alone, killing, injuring, or leaving missing nearly a dozen crew members, according to U.S. Central Command.

## Why the Bab el-Mandeb Matters

If Hormuz is the gate to the Persian Gulf, Bab el-Mandeb is the gate to the Red Sea and the Suez Canal. Between 10 and 12 percent of all seaborne-traded oil passes through this 20-mile-wide chokepoint every day. Saudi oil exports, European-bound container traffic, and a massive share of India's westbound trade all depend on it.

When the Houthis attacked commercial shipping in the Red Sea beginning in late 2023, major carriers rerouted vessels around the Cape of Good Hope, adding weeks to transit times and billions to global shipping costs. The disruption lasted nearly two years before a ceasefire in early 2026.

Now, with the Iran-U.S. conflict escalating again, the Houthis are signaling they are ready to resume.

Mohammed al-Farah, a member of the Houthi political bureau, warned this week that if Saudi Arabia continued to strike Yemen, the consequences would be severe. "If the current situation aggravates, the Bab el-Mandeb Strait and the Strait of Hormuz will be closed in an operational alliance," he said, according to Iran's Press TV. "Oil prices would then skyrocket to $200 a barrel in a dreadful shock."

The warning followed Saudi-backed strikes on a Houthi-controlled airport in Sanaa on Monday, breaking a four-year truce between the kingdom and the Iran-aligned group. Houthi forces responded with missile attacks on Saudi territory.

## What This Means for India

India's shipping and energy architecture was never designed for a world where both Hormuz and Bab el-Mandeb are contested simultaneously.

When the Hormuz crisis intensified in recent months, India and its Gulf trading partners began leaning more heavily on Red Sea routes. A tanker controlled by Abu Dhabi's national oil company transited the strait between July 10 and 12 heading for Dahej port in Gujarat, according to ship-tracking data from Kpler. Container traffic has been rerouted through Saudi ports on the Red Sea.

If Bab el-Mandeb closes, those alternatives collapse. India's trade with Europe, North Africa, and the eastern Mediterranean — much of it routed through the Suez Canal — would face massive delays and cost increases. Indian exports, which rose 15 percent in April-June despite the Gulf disruptions, could face a sharp reversal.

For the roughly nine million Indians living and working in the Gulf states, the escalation raises fresh safety concerns. The Gulf region has been under intermittent missile and drone fire for months. Iran has struck U.S. bases in Bahrain, Kuwait, and Jordan. The IRGC claimed to have set fire to a U.S. logistics facility in Kuwait's Mina Abdullah and struck aircraft hangars at Azraq in Jordan.

## The Diplomatic Calculus

Analysts say Iran is using the twin chokepoint threat as leverage — not necessarily to close Bab el-Mandeb immediately, but to make Washington think twice about further escalation.

"Iran is willing to go all the way," Fawaz Gerges, a Middle East scholar, told Reuters. Tehran is showing Washington it could threaten both chokepoints simultaneously, "transforming the conflict from a bilateral confrontation into a challenge to the sea lanes underpinning global energy trade."

Andreas Krieg of King's College London described the Houthi option as "another nuclear option" for Iran — one it would deploy only if the IRGC concluded all-out war had become unavoidable.

Dennis Ross, a former U.S. Middle East peace negotiator, framed the challenge from Washington's perspective: "The issue is, how do you change the Iranian calculus to the point where they're ready, again, to talk, but not just to talk, but actually to work out an arrangement that is acceptable."

Meanwhile, Gulf states are scrambling to build alternatives. Saudi Arabia is considering expanding its crude oil pipeline capacity to the Red Sea to nine million barrels per day. The UAE is planning a new port and container terminal on the Arabian Sea side of Hormuz. Iraq has begun construction on a pipeline to bypass the strait entirely.

But none of these projects will be ready for months or years. The immediate reality is that the world's two most critical oil chokepoints are now both under threat — and for India, there is no third route.

Oil prices rose on Wednesday to a one-month high, with Brent crude closing at its highest level since mid-June. For Indian families already dealing with rising fuel and cooking gas prices, the worst may not be over.
